description: We are a team of three looking to discover stuff!!!
summary: Night Light Trend Detective is a web tool that turns students and the public into data detectives for light pollution. Using NASA's Black Marble night-time lights (VIIRS Day/Night Band, 2012–2025), users pick a region, see how its night-time brightness changed year by year, and get a clear statistical verdict: the rate of change (Theil–Sen slope, in radiance units and % per year) and whether the trend is significant (Mann–Kendall test, p < 0.05). A per-pixel trend map then shows exactly where lights grew or faded, revealing that one region can brighten in some places and dim in others. We demonstrate it on Ho Chi Minh City, Hanoi and the dragon fruit farms of Binh Thuan (including Ham Thuan Bac, the only area of central and southern Vietnam where night lights fell significantly), where fields are lit all night to make the plants flower out of season, so light pollution there comes from agriculture rather than cities. Light at night affects ecosystems, human health, energy use and our view of the stars; our tool turns NASA data into testable evidence of how it is changing.
details:
What it does

Night Light Trend Detective answers the four questions of the challenge for one Earth-observation variable, night-time light radiance:

What is changing? Upward night-time radiance measured by NASA's VIIRS Day/Night Band (Black Marble VNP46A4 annual product).

Where? Users choose a region (Ho Chi Minh City, Hanoi, Binh Thuan dragon fruit farms, and the Ham Thuan Bac dragon fruit belt). A per-pixel trend map (~500 m pixels) shows where lights increased (red) or decreased (blue) significantly, and grey where there is no significant trend.

How much? The Theil–Sen slope gives the rate in nW/cm²/sr per year and in % per year.

Is it significant? The Mann–Kendall test gives a p-value; below 0.05 the trend is called statistically significant at 95% confidence.

Users can select four variables derived from the same NASA layer: average night brightness, lit area (% of pixels brighter than 5 nW/cm²/sr, a proxy for sprawl), brightness of areas that were already bright in 2012, and brightness of areas that were dark in 2012. A comparison table shows how the same variable trends in each region. Users can change the start and end year; the Mann–Kendall test and Sen's slope are recomputed live in the browser. This teaches an important scientific lesson: whether a trend is "significant" depends on the length of the record, and short windows can be cherry-picked. Ten guided "detective cases" walk new users through these ideas with real examples.

Key findings (2012–2025)

Ho Chi Minh City: average night radiance rose from 6.5 to 12.6 nW/cm²/sr (+0.54 per year, +5.3%/yr, Mann–Kendall p < 0.001). Lit area grew from 33% to 64% of the region; 92% of pixels brightened significantly and 0.8% dimmed. Areas that were dark in 2012 brightened about 4 times faster (+9.9%/yr) than areas already bright (+2.3%/yr). Since 2019 the trend is no longer significant (p = 0.072).

Hanoi: average radiance rose from 4.4 to 11.3 nW/cm²/sr (+0.53 per year, +6.8%/yr, p < 0.001). Lit area grew from 22% to 65%; 94% of pixels brightened significantly.

Binh Thuan dragon fruit farms: no significant trend over 2012–2025 (p = 0.91) because brightness rose and then fell: +7.4%/yr from 2012 to 2019 (p = 0.004), peaking at 57.7 nW/cm²/sr, then a sharp drop in 2022 and −8.3%/yr since 2019 (not yet significant, p = 0.072). Opposite trends inside the region: the brightest farm areas of 2012 dimmed (−3.9%/yr, p = 0.049) while areas that were dark brightened (+7.7%/yr, p = 0.009). We compared this with independent reports: the 2022 drop coincides with China's border restrictions (late 2021–2022), when farm-gate prices fell to 500–4,000 VND/kg against a break-even of 7,000–10,000 VND/kg, and with a fall in Binh Thuan dragon fruit area from 33,750 ha (2021) to about 27,900 ha at the end of 2022 (−17%). Our lit area fell 12% and brightness 35% in the same year. Brightness falling more than area is consistent with fewer fields plus less off-season lighting and more efficient bulbs (a 2021–2023 project replaced compact bulbs with 80,000 9 W LEDs). These reports make the explanation consistent with the data; satellite data alone cannot prove the cause.

Ham Thuan Bac dragon fruit belt (a zoom-in on Binh Thuan): we scanned every 0.1° cell of central and southern Vietnam (10–20°N) with the Mann–Kendall test, and only three cells showed a significant decline, all in this belt. Average radiance fell from 104.6 to 60.8 nW/cm²/sr (−6.0 per year, −5.4%/yr, p = 0.021), and by −14.6%/yr since 2019 (p = 0.035). The lit area did not shrink (77% to 84%, no significant trend), so fields stayed lit but got dimmer, which fits a switch to more efficient bulbs or shorter lighting better than abandoned fields.

How it works

A Python script downloads Black Marble VNP46A4 Collection 2 HDF5 tiles (h28v06, h28v07) from NASA LAADS DAAC using an Earthdata token, reads the `AllAngle_Composite_Snow_Free` layer (moonlight-, atmosphere- and snow-corrected), applies the scale factor and fill values, clips each region and discards the raw tiles.

An analysis script builds the annual mean radiance series per region, runs the Mann–Kendall test and Theil–Sen slope, and repeats the same test for every pixel (vectorised) to produce the trend maps.

Results are exported to JSON and PNG and shown in a static web page (HTML/JavaScript, Chart.js) hosted on GitHub Pages, with a hand-written Mann–Kendall/Theil–Sen implementation for the interactive period selector.

Benefits and intended impact

Students and the public can investigate a real environmental question with real NASA data and learn what "statistically significant" means, with plain-language definitions of every term.

Agricultural and energy agencies can track night lighting used in farming (e.g., Binh Thuan dragon fruit fields), which affects energy use, insects and nearby ecosystems.

City planners and energy agencies can see where urban lighting is growing fastest.

Non-significant results are presented as "not enough evidence yet", encouraging longer records rather than over-claiming.

Creativity and factors considered

Framed as a detective story in four steps: choose a place → look at the evidence → verdict → where exactly.

Pixel-level significance maps and the "already bright vs. dark in 2012" variables reveal opposite trends inside the same region, the twist described in the challenge: in Binh Thuan the brightest dragon fruit areas dimmed significantly while dark areas brightened significantly.

We include agricultural light pollution (dragon fruit farms), not only cities, and we report a boom-then-decline pattern honestly as "no single significant trend" instead of forcing a linear verdict.

We separate what the data show from why: trends show what changed, and we test explanations against independent reports (market prices, crop area, bulb changes) with sources listed on the website.

We explicitly communicate data limitations: VIIRS DNB is not sensitive to blue LED light below ~500 nm (so cities and farms switching to white LEDs can look darker), it observes at ~01:30 local time, and it measures upward radiance rather than ground-level sky glow. Annual composites avoid seasonal cycles, so no de-seasonalising is needed, and we test monotonic (linear) trends only.

Tools

Python (h5py, NumPy, SciPy, pymannkendall, Matplotlib, requests), HTML/CSS/JavaScript, Chart.js, Git, GitHub Pages.
